Okay, let's try to figure out which of these four options is the odd one out in terms of conceptual meaning. First, I need to understand each couplet's theme.

Starting with option 1: "دی در گذار بود و نظر سوی ما نکرد - بیچاره دل که هیچ ندید از گذار عمر"  
Translating roughly, it's saying that Dey (a month in the Persian calendar) was passing, but the person didn't look our way. The poor heart saw nothing from the passing of life's Dey. So this seems to be about the passage of time (Dey symbolizing time here) and unfulfilled longing or missed opportunities. The message is about the futility of waiting or the transience of time without achieving what one desires.

Option 2: "گفتم غم تو دارم گفتا غمت سرآید - گفتم که ماه من شو گفتا اگر برآید"  
This one is a dialogue. The speaker says, "I have your sorrow," and the other replies, "Your sorrow has come to an end." Then the speaker says, "Let me be your moon," and the other says, "If it rises." The moon here might be a symbol of hope or a beloved. The exchange seems to involve unrequited love or a response that is conditional or uncertain. The message is about the complexity of emotions and perhaps not getting the desired response.

Option 3: "دی می شد و گفتم صنما عهد به جای آر - گفتا غلطی خواجه در این عهد وفا نیست"  
Again, Dey is mentioned, so time is a theme. The speaker says, "Dey was coming and I said the promise would be fulfilled," but the other says, "O master, you made a mistake; there is no faithfulness in this promise." So here, the speaker is expecting a promise to be kept (maybe in the context of time passing), but the response is disappointment in the broken promise. The theme is about broken promises and the failure of someone to uphold their word, especially as time goes by.

Option 4: "ز محبتت نخواهم که نظر کنم به رویت - که محب صادق آن است که پاکباز باشد"  
This one is different. The speaker is saying, "I don't want your love that makes me look at your face," and adds, "The true lover is the one who is chaste." The message here seems to be about the nature of true love, emphasizing chastity and perhaps the idea that genuine love doesn't require physical presence or desire. It's more about the virtue of the lover rather than the passage of time or broken promises.

Now, looking at the common themes. Options 1, 2, and 3 all seem to deal with time (Dey as a month, the passing of time) and unfulfilled expectations or disappointments. Option 1 talks about not seeing anything in the passing of life's Dey. Option 2 has a conditional response, maybe not fully fulfilling the speaker's hope. Option 3 directly mentions a promise not being kept as Dey approaches. 

Option 4, on the other hand, is about the characteristics of true love and chastity. It's not about the passage of time or broken promises but rather about the moral aspect of love. So the deviation here is that Option 4 is focusing on the virtue of the lover (being chaste) rather than the themes of time and unfulfilled expectations present in the others.
